questions.question: What does the Complex Conjugate Root Theorem say for a polynomial with real coefficients?
options: If a + ib is a root, then a - ib is also a root.
If a + ib is a root, then -a + ib is also a root.
Every root of the polynomial must be real.
Every real polynomial has only two complex roots.

questions.question: In the complex conjugate root theorem, what condition on the polynomial is essential?
options: The polynomial must have integer coefficients.
The polynomial must have degree two.
The polynomial must have no real roots.
The polynomial must have real coefficients.

A real polynomial has -1 - 4i as a root. Which root is guaranteed by the complex conjugate root theorem?
What is meant by the interpretation that complex roots of real polynomials come in pairs?
options: Every real root has a distinct real partner.
Every non-real complex root is accompanied by its complex conjugate.
Every polynomial with real coefficients has exactly two roots.

questions.question: Why does the complex conjugate root theorem help explain why an odd-degree real polynomial must have at least one real root?
options: Non-real roots occur in pairs, leaving a real root in odd degree.
Because a non-real root forces its negative to be a root.
Because every odd-degree polynomial has exactly one real root.
Because each conjugate pair counts as one root.

questions.question: A real polynomial has roots 1 + 2i and 3 - i. Which two roots are also guaranteed?
A real polynomial of degree 3 has one non-real root 4 + i. Which statement must be true?
options: The polynomial has no real roots.

questions.question: Which situation is not covered by the Complex Conjugate Root Theorem?
options: A polynomial in one variable with real coefficients.
A real polynomial with a non-real root.
A real polynomial whose root is a + ib with a and b real.

questions.question: How does the complex conjugate root theorem treat a real root written as a + ib?
options: It is outside the theorem because a and b must be non-zero.
It gives the same root again when b = 0.
It forces a second distinct real root.
It shows that the polynomial has no non-real roots.

questions.question: A real polynomial has exactly three roots counted with multiplicity. Two of them are 2 + i and 2 - i. What can be concluded about the remaining root?
A real square matrix has odd size. What can be concluded about its eigenvalues?
options: It has at least one real eigenvalue.
Its non-real eigenvalues cannot occur in conjugate pairs.

questions.question: Which coefficient condition is needed in the Complex Conjugate Root Theorem?
options: The polynomial has only imaginary coefficients.
The polynomial has degree exactly two.
The polynomial has no real roots.

What pattern do non-real roots of a real polynomial follow?
options: They occur only on the imaginary axis.
They must all be positive real numbers.
They cannot occur in odd-degree polynomials.

options: Every complex root is automatically real.
Non-real roots are paired, so an odd total number of roots leaves at least one real root.
Odd-degree polynomials cannot have complex roots, no matter which values are selected.
The conjugate of every root is zero.
